function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can follow to get the repository ready for deployment.  
I’ll walk you through what you need to do locally, and I’ll provide the exact files you’ll need to add/modify.

> **NOTE** – I’m unable to run `git` commands or push to the remote repository from here, so you’ll have to execute those steps yourself on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Create Required Files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image as the base
FROM node:18-slim

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first (if present)
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *Why this Dockerfile?*  
> - It uses a lightweight Node.js image.  
> - `npm ci` ensures reproducible builds.  
> - The app is assumed to listen on port `3000` (adjust if your app uses a different port).

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory called `k8s` (or `deployments`, whatever you prefer) and add two files:

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> *What to replace:*  
> - `<YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>` – e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq` if you’re using GitHub Container Registry.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/docker-image.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build and Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest .
          docker tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}

      # Push the Docker image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
```

> *What this does:*  
> - Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> - Builds a Docker image tagged `latest` and with the commit SHA.  
> - Pushes both tags to GitHub Container Registry.

---

## 3️⃣ Add All Changed Files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/docker-image.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

### Quick Checklist

| Step | Action | Done? |
|------|--------|-------|
| 1 | Clone repo | ✅ |
| 2.1 | Create Dockerfile | ✅ |
| 2.2 | Create Kubernetes YAMLs | ✅ |
| 2.3 | Create GitHub Actions workflow | ✅ |
| 3 | Add files to git | ✅ |
| 4 | Commit & push | ✅ |

Once pushed, GitHub Actions will automatically build and publish your Docker image. You can then deploy the Kubernetes manifests to your cluster using `kubectl apply -f k8s/`.

Happy coding! 🚀
